extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and constitutional law; policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and evaluative guidance on forms, procedures, advantages and disadvantages of direct legislation (initiative, referendum, local option) as applied in U.S. States and by comparison to Swiss/French practice. Covers procedural thresholds, constitutional placement of issues, and practical effects on legislatures and voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid placing ordinary law in the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of putting into the Constitution matters proper for an ordinary statute embarrasses a legislature by raising questions of its competence and of agreement between its acts and the directions contained in the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing private law and administrative regulation with the frame of government causes confusion; it heightens difficulty of correcting mistakes because amending a constitution is slow, and leaves blemishes tolerated which a sovereign legislature could remedy quickly. (Page discussion: 'inconvenient as well as unscientific mixture...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment ratification quorum/majority requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a majority of all the qualified voters, and not merely of those voting, is required to affirm an amendment it often happens that the requisite majority cannot be obtained owing to the small number who vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High quorum/majority rules act as a check on hasty or frequent change but make correcting even admitted evils practically irremovable because the mass of people may not be induced to vote. (Example: happened in Kentucky and Delaware.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative and referendum petition thresholds and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiative and Referendum powers require specified proportions of voters to propose measures or to demand submission of laws (e.g. Oklahoma: 8% to propose laws, 15% to propose constitutional amendments; 5% to demand a referendum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given from Oklahoma, Swiss Federal Constitution, and other states; referendums may be ordered by petition or by the legislature; the referendum may be demanded against items or parts of a bill; the Governor's veto typically does not extend to measures voted by the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swiss-style referendum for ordinary laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission to the people for their approval or rejection of ordinary laws passed by the State Legislature (the true Swiss Referendum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Switzerland and adopted in varying degree by several U.S. States; differs from American practice that often places subjects into the constitution rather than submitting ordinary laws after passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative power to propose laws or constitutional amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: A power for a certain proportion of voters to propose either ordinary laws or amendments to the State Constitution (the Swiss Initiative model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States vary in required signature percentages and procedures; Oregon and Oklahoma are given as examples where many initiatives have been submitted and decided by popular vote (Oregon: 76 initiatives to 1912, 33 carried, 43 rejected). Initiative use can greatly extend direct popular control over legislation and constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local option (local referendums for municipal matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting to the direct vote of the inhabitants of a town or local area the enactment of an ordinance affecting that district (e.g. whether to levy a rate for a free library or grant liquor licences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local option differs from Swiss referendum in being locally restricted and in deciding whether a general Act shall operate in a given area; courts differ on the extent to which legislatures may refer operation of laws to local popular vote, but the weight of authority supports local option laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit executive veto over popular measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The veto power of the Governor is not to extend to measures voted on by the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Oklahoma and Oregon — the Governor has no veto on popular votes; measures enacted by direct vote are final without executive override.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect constitutional permanence versus risk of mutability
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of Initiative and Referendum can remove the sense of permanence from a constitution and make provisions as mutable as ordinary statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If constitutions are recast or amended often by popular vote, the conservative advantage of a rigid constitution disappears and ordinary laws may be passed under momentary impulse; this is a chief objection though mitigated in large democracies and by the view that reference to the people may sometimes act as a conservative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce legislative corruption and special-interest influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct legislation is defended on the ground that the mass of the people are less exposed to temptations and cannot be 'got at' in the way individual legislators can be; therefore people can reject measures passed under special influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argued as a practical advantage when legislatures are timid or easily swayed by active sections of opinion; cited as reason for extending direct vote powers to counter bribery, 'log-rolling', and lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overburdening voters (the Ballot's Burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying initiative/referendum to many local or administrative questions may impose on the average voter a heavier burden than his knowledge and capacity fit him to bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: Portland (1909) where an elector faced 25 candidates plus 35 separate legislative propositions; warns against excessive use of direct votes on detailed administrative matters (citation: Professor Beard, The Ballot's Burden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve certain financial/major public decisions to popular approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Some state constitutions require popular approval for certain financial actions (e.g. contracting debts beyond a specified amount, appropriating certain funds, changing the seat of government, or increases in taxation rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Minnesota (approval needed for certain railway laws and appropriation of internal improvement land fund), California (seat of State government change requires people's approval); this withdraws some traditional legislative functions to popular control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature should not delegate core law-making power (Delegata potestas non delegatur)
rubrics_metrics.description: One settled maxim is that the power conferred upon the legislature to make laws cannot be delegated by that department to any other body or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine complicates the relation between representative law-making and submission to popular vote: while some American courts strictly enforce it, British practice allows broader delegation; careful constitutional design is needed to reconcile delegation principles with initiative/referendum practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use popular vote where legislatures are unwilling or unable to act on divisive issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures have sometimes referred questions (e.g. liquor traffic, location of state capital, prison-made articles sale) to the people because members prefer to avoid embarrassing or divisive problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice both relieved legislatures and helped to legitimize decisions on contentious local issues; it exemplifies a functional criterion for when to employ direct legislation (i.e., where representative bodies are paralyzed or have strong local/special interests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for submitting constitutional proposals to local assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical mechanism (e.g. French 1793 model): any law proposed by the legislative body shall be published and sent to communes whose primary assemblies shall be convoked to vote upon it if objections are raised by a fraction of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates a procedural safeguard ensuring local dissemination and deliberation; used as a comparative point showing variations in how direct input can be organized (publication, convocation, thresholds for triggering local consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to demand federal referendum by a defined minority (Swiss example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swiss Federal Constitution: any Federal law and Federal resolution not urgent must, on the demand of eight cantons or of 30,000 voters, be submitted to popular vote for acceptance or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a concrete model of minority-triggered referendum at the federal level and shows one way to balance representative law-making with popular control; cited as an instructive comparative provision.
